doc.title: Allan Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Not knowing tunes at gigs and the supportive spirit
summary: Players regularly face unfamiliar tunes, especially bebop heads; musicians help each other.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: What is the likelihood of when you come to these gigs that you get in a situation where you don’t know enough tunes.
Oh, constantly. Constantly. We all have the same situation.
Just as an observer, from what I’ve seen it always seem like you guys aren’t at a loss but I’m almost glad to hear that you’re human in that sense.

Oh sure, sure. This weekend I was a little concerned because there’s a lot of what I would consider more contemporary, modern players here at this, than I’m used to doing on these things. And I’m somewhat a little concerned that the guys are going to start calling up some heavy bebop things and I’m going to say gee guys, I don’t really know those. And it’s not that I haven’t heard them, it’s just that I never really took the time to learn them because I never really had to before.
Yeah, and the heads on those tunes can be —

Yeah, you’ve got to play them exact otherwise it’s not right. I’d really have to sit down and practice a little bit. But you know generally, the thing about this is everybody is — nobody is out to get anybody else. We’re not out to see if we can nail this guy or nail that guy. We’re all here to have a good time and try to celebrate the music as best as we can and present it in the best possible way to the audience who is paying the bills for us to see. So I mean we’ll all get together — if one guy says well gee I really don’t know that tune, they’ll say okay, well let’s pick something else.
